name: Goguryeo
summary: One of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, ruling northern Korea and much of Manchuria. It fought off huge Sui and Tang invasions before falling to a Silla–Tang alliance in 668.

location.value: Northern and central Korea and much of Manchuria, possibly reaching eastern Mongolia.

terrain.value: Mountains and river valleys (Yalu, Liao), ideal for fortresses.

climate.value: Cold continental: long, cold winters and warm summers.

resources.value: Iron, horses, timber and farmland in the river valleys.

disasters.value: Unknown in detail; the Samguk sagi mentions droughts, locusts and famines.

population.value: About 3.5 million (Wikipedia comparison with Baekje and Silla).

urbanisation.value: Pyongyang became the capital in 427; earlier capitals were in the mountains along the Yalu River.

migration.value: Refugees went to Balhae and Silla after its fall.

economicBase.value: The page gives no economic overview: the mountainous land lacked arable land, and Goguryeo relied on tribute from conquered tribes and raids on neighbours.

tradeRoutes.value: Contact with Chinese states, the northern steppe and the other Korean kingdoms.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; royal tombs show great wealth.

moneyAndTax.value: Taxes paid in grain and cloth; no coinage of its own is known.

inequality.value: Ruled by aristocratic clans; slaves and commoners at the bottom.

governmentType.value: A monarchy with powerful aristocrats, centralised over time.

keyRulers.value: Jumong founded the kingdom in 37 BCE (a date the page says is in doubt; the infobox lists Dongmyeong as first king); Gwanggaeto the Great 391–413 (391–412 in one place); Jangsu 413–491, who ruled 79 years and moved the capital to Pyongyang in 427.

succession.value: Hereditary in the royal Go family; at first sometimes brother to brother, later father to son.

institutions.value: An aristocratic council and ranks of officials; the Taehak academy (372).

stability.value: Strong for centuries, until internal strife and Tang–Silla attacks in the 660s.

eliteConflict.value: After Yeon Gaesomun died (about 666), his sons fought each other, weakening the state.

majorWars.value: Sui mobilised about 1,133,800 combat troops in 612 and was trapped at the Battle of Salsu, where only about 2,700 escaped; Tang Emperor Taizong attacked in 645 and again in 647 and 648 and was defeated; a Silla–Tang alliance took Pyongyang in 668.

territoryChange.value: At its peak most of Korea and large parts of Manchuria.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Baekje, Silla, Sui and Tang China.

inventions.value: Ondol underfloor heating is linked to the region.

scienceEducation.value: A national academy (Taehak) was founded in 372 to teach Confucian classics.

openness.value: Adopted Buddhism from China in 372 and borrowed Chinese writing and law.

communicationTransport.value: Horses for travel and war; mountain fortresses guarding routes; roads to China.

religion.value: Buddhism was introduced in 372 and encouraged by the government; Korean shamanism was an integral part of the culture.

languageWriting.value: The Goguryeo language (little is known); records were written in Chinese characters.

artsArchitecture.value: Painted tomb murals of hunters, dancers and the four guardian animals (World Heritage Sites).

socialStructure.value: Royal family, aristocrats, commoners and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Claimed descent from the Buyeo people and the founder Jumong.

dailyLife.value: Houses with ondol (under-floor heating); millet, beans and meat; tomb murals show kitchens and stables.

neighbours.value: Baekje, Silla, Buyeo, Chinese dynasties and steppe peoples.

ideasReligions.value: Passed Buddhism and Chinese learning on to Japan (for example the monk Hyeja).

colonisation.value: None overseas; it expanded on land into Manchuria.

riseSignals.value: Founded in 37 BCE according to tradition, near the Yalu River.

peakPeriod.value: Under Gwanggaeto and Jangsu the kingdom held about three-quarters of the Korean peninsula and almost all of Manchuria; the page gives no single peak year.

declineSignals.value: Long wars with the Sui and Tang (598–668) drained its strength.

outcome.value: Fell to an alliance of Silla and Tang China in 668; refugees later helped found Balhae (698).

knownFor.label: Gwanggaeto Stele
knownFor.note: A huge stone recording his conquests.

knownFor.label: Mountain fortresses
knownFor.note: Stone forts that held off Sui and Tang.
